title: Check yourself: heap, stack and Metaspace

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: An XML import recurses once per nesting level. On platform threads with -Xss1m it failed with StackOverflowError on a document nested 40,000 levels deep. The team moves the import onto virtual threads, whose frames are copied to the heap when they unmount with the same JVM options. What happens with the same document?

options.text: It succeeds, since a virtual thread's stack can keep growing as long as the heap has room
options.says: -Xss caps the virtual thread's depth; the heap's size doesn't raise it

options.text: It succeeds, since -Xss sizes only platform threads and a virtual thread's stack grows on the heap
options.says: -Xss caps a virtual thread's depth too: on the page it went 9,818 frames deep against 9,835 for a platform thread

options.text: It fails at about the same depth, since -Xss also caps how deep a virtual thread's stack can grow
options.says: a virtual thread's frames live on the heap while it is unmounted, but its depth is capped by -Xss like a platform thread's (9,818 vs 9,835 frames on the page)

options.text: It fails at a smaller depth, since a virtual thread's stack stays at a few kilobytes while it runs
options.says: a virtual thread's stack grows as it calls deeper, up to the -Xss cap; the page's virtual thread went as deep as the platform thread

origin.section: -Xss Sets How Many Frames Fit, So Recursion as Deep as the Data Fails on Large Input

questions.stem: A report service fails with OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space. The stack trace ends in CsvWriter.grow, which copies an 8 MB buffer into a 16 MB one. CsvWriter is created per report; the service keeps user sessions in a static map. A teammate makes CsvWriter start with a 16 MB buffer so that it never grows; the error stops for a week, then returns. What best explains that?

options.text: CsvWriter still holds most of the heap, and a week of reports later its 16 MB buffer was too small again
options.says: the trace names the allocation that failed, not what holds the memory; CsvWriter's buffers are garbage once a report is done

options.text: The session map holds most of the heap, and a week later its expired sessions were still too new for the collector to clear
options.says: the collector frees what nothing reachable refers to, whatever its age; the map still refers to every session

options.text: CsvWriter still holds most of the heap, and a week of reports later its unflushed buffers had piled up again
options.says: a CsvWriter and its buffer are garbage once its report is done; the trace names the allocation that failed, not what holds the memory

options.text: The session map holds most of the heap, and a week of sessions later another allocation was the one that failed
options.says: the error is thrown by whichever allocation fails; the sessions stay reachable and keep growing, so another allocation fails next

origin.section: OutOfMemoryError Is Thrown by Whichever Allocation Fails, Not by the Code That Filled the Heap

questions.stem: A cache service runs with -Xmx30g. To make room for 20% more entries, it is restarted with -Xmx36g. How many entries fit now, compared with before?

options.text: Fewer than 20% more, since every object header grows from 12 to 16 bytes above 32 GB
options.says: the header stays 12 bytes with compressed oops off: an object with one int is 16 bytes either way on the page

options.text: Fewer than 20% more, since every reference in the heap now takes 8 bytes instead of 4
options.says: from -Xmx32g up the JVM turns compressed oops off, so every reference field and array slot doubles

options.text: About 20% more, since the extra 6 GB holds entries of the same size as before
options.says: the entries get bigger, because their references go from 4 to 8 bytes

options.text: About 20% more, since compressed oops stay on while the machine has enough memory
options.says: compressed oops depend on the heap size, not the machine's memory: -Xmx32g turns them off

origin.section: An Object Costs a Header Plus Its Fields, Rounded Up to 8 Bytes; a Reference Costs 4 Bytes Below 32 GB

questions.stem: A pricing method creates a Window record from two longs, calls window.contains(ts) and returns the boolean. The warmed-up service's allocation profile shows no Window objects. A later change adds one line, metrics.observe(window), where metrics is an interface with several implementations in use, so that call site isn't inlined. What does the profile show after the change?

options.text: No Window objects, since a call that isn't inlined can't keep a reference to the record it receives
options.says: code the compiler can't see might store the reference, so the analysis must treat the record as escaping

options.text: A Window per call, since a method with a call that isn't inlined is no longer compiled by C2
options.says: the method is still compiled; only objects that reach code the analysis can't see escape, as the page shows with the constructor kept out of inlining

options.text: A Window per call, since the record is passed to code that isn't inlined into the method
options.says: escape analysis sees only inlined code, so an argument to a call that isn't inlined counts as escaping, and the allocation comes back

options.text: No Window objects, since the record is passed to observe() as its two fields rather than as an object
options.says: a call the compiler can't see into receives a real reference, so the record must exist on the heap

origin.section: Escape Analysis Can Remove an Allocation, but Only in Compiled Code and Only While the Object Stays Local

questions.stem: A rules engine compiles each rule into a hidden class and caches the classes in a map whose key includes the request id. It runs with -Xmx4g, and after two days it fails with OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace. Operations restarts it with -Xmx8g. What happens next?

options.text: It runs about twice as long, since the map's classes are stored in the heap, which the restart doubles
options.says: class metadata lives in Metaspace, native memory outside the heap; the page's run failed with 3 MB of a 1 GB heap in use

options.text: It fails again after about two days, since its hidden classes stay loaded until the JVM exits, mapped or not
options.says: hidden classes are unloaded once nothing reaches them; on the page 299,159 of 300,000 dropped classes were

options.text: It runs about twice as long, since Metaspace is sized from the heap, so the map's classes get twice the room
options.says: Metaspace is limited by MaxMetaspaceSize, not by -Xmx

options.text: It fails again after about two days, since the map keeps its classes reachable and Metaspace is outside the heap
options.says: class metadata is in Metaspace, which -Xmx doesn't bound, and the map keeps every class reachable so none is unloaded

concepts: References are 4 bytes through compressed oops up to a 32 GB heap; from -Xmx32g the JVM turns them off and every reference field and array slot doubles, while the header stays 12 bytes.

C2's escape analysis removes the allocation of an object that provably stays local in compiled code; a field store, or a call the JIT doesn't inline, makes it escape, and HotSpot never puts the object on the stack instead.
Class metadata lives in Metaspace, outside -Xmx and unlimited by default; generated classes kept reachable exhaust it with the heap nearly empty, and unreachable hidden classes are unloaded.
OutOfMemoryError is thrown by the allocation that failed, so the trace names the victim rather than what holds the memory, and a bigger heap only moves the failure while the holder keeps growing.
A virtual thread's frames go to the heap when it unmounts, but -Xss caps its depth as it caps a platform thread's; one platform thread can get its own stack size.
